title: Units, dimensions and prefixes
summary: Units, prefixes and dimensions let everyone state and check measurements the same way.

layers.basics: Volts, amps, ohms, farads and henries are units; prefixes like milli- and mega- scale them. Checking units catches many mistakes.
layers.deeper: Dimensional analysis shows that RC has units of seconds and that √(L/C) has units of ohms.
layers.expert: SI base units include the ampere (defined via the elementary charge e=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C since 2019); decibels express ratios logarithmically: dB=20log₁₀(V₂/V₁).

formula: dB = 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁) for voltage ratios at equal impedance; 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁) for power

title: Kinematics and forces
summary: Describing motion and what causes it.

layers.basics: Position, velocity and acceleration describe motion; Newton’s laws link acceleration to force.
layers.deeper: For constant acceleration, x=x₀+v₀t+½at² and v=v₀+at. Mechanical systems (motors, MEMS springs, loudspeaker cones) are modelled with the same equations as circuits.
layers.expert: F=ma; the mass–spring–damper mẍ+bẋ+kx=F is the mechanical twin of series RLC (m↔L, b↔R, k↔1/C).

formula: F_net = m a (constant mass, speeds much less than c; in general F = dp/dt)

layers.basics: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only moved; power is energy per time; the momentum of a system is conserved whenever no net external force acts, as in collisions.
layers.deeper: Electric power P=VI is the same idea as mechanical power P=Fv, and electromagnetic fields carry energy and momentum too.
layers.expert: Work–energy theorem W_net=ΔKE; potential energy of conservative forces; the Poynting vector S=E×B/μ₀ integrated over a closed surface (∯S·dA) gives the net rate at which field energy flows out.

layers.basics: Torque twists things the way force pushes them; moment of inertia is rotational mass.
layers.deeper: Electric motors and generators convert between electrical power and torque×speed.
layers.expert: τ=Iα; rotational power P=τω; angular momentum L=Iω conserved without external torque; spinning-rotor gyroscopes rely on conserved angular momentum, while MEMS gyros sense rotation by the Coriolis force on a vibrating proof mass. L=Iω holds for rotation about a principal axis.

title: Charge and Coulomb’s law
summary: Charges push or pull with an inverse-square force.

layers.basics: Like charges repel, unlike attract, and the force falls with the square of distance.
layers.deeper: Charge is conserved, and any isolated charge is a whole multiple of e (quarks carry thirds of e but are never found alone). Electric field is force per unit charge.
layers.expert: F=kq₁q₂/r², k=1/(4πε₀)≈8.988×10⁹ N·m²/C². Superposition holds, which is why fields of many charges add as vectors.

facts: ≈8.988×10⁹ N·m²/C² (computed from the CODATA 2022 value of ε₀)
formula: F = q₁q₂ / (4πε₀ r²) (static point charges, vacuum; positive = repulsion)

title: Gauss’s law
summary: Electric flux out of a closed surface counts the enclosed charge.

layers.basics: Surround any region with an imaginary surface: the net electric flux passing out is proportional to the charge inside.
layers.deeper: For symmetric charge shapes it gives the field directly. In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero, and Gauss’s law then shows that any net charge sits on its surface.

title: Electric potential and voltage
summary: Energy per charge: what we call voltage.

layers.basics: Voltage is the energy a unit charge gains moving between two points; a battery maintains a voltage.
layers.deeper: Potential is a scalar map of the field; equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines. Ground is a chosen zero.
layers.expert: V=−∫E·dl; point charge V=q/4πε₀r; Poisson ∇²V=−ρ/ε₀. Voltage differences are path independent only while the magnetic flux through the loop is constant; with changing flux (inductors, transformers) the electric field is not conservative and ∮E·dl=−dΦ_B/dt.

title: Capacitance and dielectrics
summary: Storing charge in an electric field.

layers.basics: Two conductors separated by an insulator hold equal and opposite charges +Q and −Q when a voltage is applied; the ratio Q/V is capacitance.
layers.deeper: A dielectric between the plates increases capacitance by the factor εr at fixed geometry; energy is stored in the field.
layers.expert: C=εA/d for parallel plates with d much smaller than the plate size (fringing neglected); U=½CV²; series 1/C=Σ1/Cᵢ; parallel C=ΣCᵢ. Molecular polarisation explains εr; dielectric breakdown limits voltage.

layers.basics: Current is charge flowing per second; resistivity says how much a material opposes it.
layers.deeper: In metals, resistance comes from electrons scattering off lattice vibrations, impurities and defects (Drude’s collision picture is the simple model), and many metals follow Ohm’s law over a wide range, though many devices, such as diodes, do not; semiconductors have far fewer carriers that can be controlled.
layers.expert: J=σE microscopic Ohm’s law; Drude model σ=nq²τ/m; R=ρL/A; resistivity rises with temperature in metals (above their superconducting transition, if any) and falls with temperature in intrinsic or lightly doped semiconductors, where thermal excitation of carriers dominates.

title: Magnetic fields and forces
summary: Moving charge feels and creates magnetic fields.

layers.basics: Moving charges and currents create magnetic fields and feel forces in them, which is how motors turn.
layers.deeper: Biot–Savart and Ampère’s law give fields of wires and coils; force on a wire is I L × B; Hall effect senses fields.
layers.expert: F=q(E+v×B); ∮B·dl=μ₀(I_enc+ε₀ dΦ_E/dt), which reduces to μ₀I_enc for steady currents; inside a long ideal solenoid B≈μ₀nI; ∇·B=0, because no magnetic monopole has ever been observed (some unified theories predict they exist).

open_questions: Do magnetic monopoles exist? None has been found; some unification theories predict them.

layers.basics: Changing the magnetic flux through a loop creates an electromotive force; the induced current opposes the change.
layers.deeper: This one law explains generators, transformers, inductors and wireless charging.
layers.expert: ε=−N dΦ_B/dt for a coil of N turns; for a stationary loop this matches ∇×E=−∂B/∂t; motional EMF ε=Blv when B, l and v are mutually perpendicular; eddy currents arise in solid conductors.

title: Inductance
summary: Storing energy in a magnetic field.

layers.basics: A coil resists changes in current because its own changing field induces a counter-voltage.
layers.deeper: Self- and mutual inductance quantify this; energy ½LI² is stored in the field.
layers.expert: v=L di/dt; L=N²μA/ℓ for a solenoid; M=k√(L₁L₂) with coupling 0≤k≤1.

layers.basics: In ordinary (linear) media waves simply add: peaks meeting peaks reinforce, and peaks meeting troughs cancel, fully so when their sizes match. Confined waves form standing patterns, and a standing wave resonates when the wavelength fits the confined space.
layers.deeper: Transmission lines, antennas, optical cavities and acoustic resonators all rely on the same ideas.
layers.expert: y=A sin(kx−ωt), v=fλ; standing waves with nodes at fixed ends: fₙ=nv/2L; phase velocity vs group velocity.

title: Optics and light
summary: Light as a ray and as a wave.

layers.basics: Light reflects, refracts and diffracts. Lenses and mirrors focus it.
layers.deeper: Snell’s law n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂ governs fibre guiding; diffraction limits resolution of photolithography.
layers.expert: Rayleigh limit θ=1.22λ/D; thin-film interference; Fresnel equations for reflectance; visible light is electromagnetic radiation of roughly 380–750 nm (the limits vary between sources); the Rayleigh limit applies to a circular aperture at small angles.

title: Photoelectric effect and photons

layers.basics: Below a threshold frequency no electrons are ejected at ordinary light intensities, however bright the light; above it, electrons come out at once. Einstein explained this with energy packets of size hf. Later work showed that a treatment with classical light acting on quantised matter also reproduces it, so other experiments, such as photon antibunching, are the stronger evidence for photons.
layers.deeper: Photon energy E=hf; the same physics runs solar cells and photodiodes.
layers.expert: K_max=hf−φ; h=6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s; absorption of a photon with E>E_g creates an electron–hole pair.

open_questions: How much of the photoelectric effect can be explained with classical light and quantised matter, and which experiments are needed to establish photons, is a long-running question in the foundations of optics.

title: Quantum mechanics: the basis of semiconductors
summary: Matter has wave properties; when confined, its allowed energies are discrete, and in crystals they merge into bands.

layers.basics: Electrons confined in atoms or crystals have only certain allowed energies. This explains why materials differ as conductors, insulators and semiconductors.
layers.deeper: Wave functions, the uncertainty principle and tunnelling are the intro to band theory and to why tiny transistors leak.
layers.expert: Time-independent Schrödinger equation −ħ²/2m ψ″+Vψ=Eψ; particle in a box Eₙ=n²π²ħ²/2mL²; Pauli exclusion fills states two electrons at a time.

title: Atomic structure and the periodic table

layers.basics: Atoms have a nucleus and electron shells. Main-group elements in the same column share valence electron counts and so behave alike.
layers.deeper: Silicon (group 14) has four valence electrons and bonds tetrahedrally in a diamond-cubic crystal; boron (group 13, three valence electrons) and phosphorus (group 15, five) are the classic p-type and n-type dopants.
layers.expert: Electron configuration, ionisation energy and electronegativity trends help explain which elements make good conductors, dopants and dielectrics. Silicon is [Ne]3s²3p²: the four outer electrons fill the 3s and 3p subshells, and an atom with one more or one fewer outer electron can donate or accept a carrier when it replaces silicon in the lattice.

title: Chemical bonding and material properties
summary: Why materials conduct, insulate or flex.

layers.basics: Metallic bonds leave electrons free to move (conductors); in many covalent and ionic solids the valence electrons are held in bonds, so the material insulates or conducts weakly (set by its band gap, and in ionic solids by mobile ions). Some covalent solids, such as graphite, still conduct.
layers.deeper: Silicon’s covalent diamond-cubic lattice has a band gap of about 1.12 eV at 300 K, small enough for doping to control conduction. Carbon in the same lattice (diamond) is a wide-gap insulator, so the gap comes from bond strength and atom size, not from the lattice type alone. SiO₂ is a strong insulator, which is why MOS gates and chip isolation work.
layers.expert: Bond strength and bond angles set band gaps and mechanical behaviour; lattice types (diamond, zincblende) matter for III-V devices; thermal conductivity and expansion drive packaging: silicon conducts heat at about 150 W/(m·K) and expands about 2.6 ppm/K at 300 K, and package materials are chosen to match.

facts: Silicon linear thermal expansion at 300 K

layers.basics: A battery turns chemical energy into electricity via oxidation at one electrode and reduction at the other.
layers.deeper: Cell voltage depends on the electrode materials; lithium-ion cells shuttle Li⁺ ions between a host anode (usually graphite) and a metal-oxide or phosphate cathode.
layers.expert: Nernst equation E=E°−(RT/nF)ln Q; capacity in Ah, internal resistance and C-rate set practical performance; degradation has several mechanisms, including growth of the solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI), lithium plating and electrode cracking. The Nernst equation gives the open-circuit voltage near equilibrium, where Q is the reaction quotient.
